summary: Sample 17Al (nominal Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu, at.%), a Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steel, in the condition aged at 575 °C for 6 h after solution treatment at 1100 °C/10 min and oil quenching, then water quenched. This condition is the peak-hardness state of the 17Al alloy, reaching 924.9 ± 25.8 HV, and was studied (along with the 15Al and 19Al siblings) to clarify how Al content governs the α→β-Mn aging transformation and the resulting ultra-high, flexible hardness of Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels.
composition: Measured (EDS) composition of the 17Al alloy: Fe 43.2, Mn 34.8, Al 17.0, Cu 5.0 at.% (Table 1). It is an Fe-based, Al- and Mn-rich low-density steel; the three alloys of the study (15Al, 17Al, 19Al) keep Mn (~35 at.%) and Cu (~5 at.%) essentially constant while Al increases from 15.0 to 18.6 at.% by substituting Al for Fe. Design intent: ~35 at.% Mn is added to promote the precipitation kinetics of the ultra-hard β-Mn phase; Cu is added because it both accelerates β-Mn precipitation and raises hardness; Al is the principal density-reducing element (about 0.1 g·cm⁻³ per 1 wt% Al) and, as the variable of the study, is targeted at tuning density and the aging-hardening behaviour. Measured density of the 17Al alloy is 6.76 g·cm⁻³ (Archimedes method), between 6.85 (15Al) and 6.66 (19Al) g·cm⁻³.
processing: Processing lineage of the 17Al alloy: (1) vacuum induction melting of high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials under an argon atmosphere to produce ingots of nominal Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu (at.%); (2) homogenization at 1200 °C for 24 h; (3) hot rolling into plates 4 mm thick; (4) electrical-discharge machining into 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ specimens for hardness measurement and microstructure characterization; (5) solution treatment (parent process) at 1100 °C for 10 min under argon followed by oil quenching; (6) the aging treatment that defines this sample — 575 °C for 6 h followed by water quenching. Specimens for Vickers testing, XRD, SEM and EBSD were electrolytically polished in 10 % perchloric acid + 90 % ethanol; TEM foils were ground to ~90 µm, punched to 3 mm discs and ion thinned. Nanoindentation samples were mechanically polished (to avoid flaking of the Cu-rich phase). This 575 °C/6 h step is one point within a broader aging matrix of 525–650 °C for 1, 3, 6 and 10 h applied to the same solution-treated material.
microstructure: After aging the 17Al alloy at 575 °C for 6 h, the α (BCC) matrix has almost completely transformed into near-equiaxed β-Mn: the EBSD phase map is essentially entirely β-Mn (green) with an equiaxed, randomly oriented (multicoloured) grain structure at the 100 µm scale, and the SE-SEM image shows a uniform matrix with dense fine dot-like precipitates in high-magnification insets. Three phases coexist: (i) the dominant β-Mn matrix (SAED indexed on [012] and [111] beams); (ii) a large amount of fine, elongated/rectangular FCC Cu-rich particles distributed at the β-Mn interfaces, frequently containing an FCC twin structure (SAED shows two superimposed twin-related patterns, "FCC twin"); and (iii) a small amount of a new BCC phase within the β-Mn, of particle size comparable to the FCC Cu-rich phase. β-Mn is an Mn-rich phase — SEM-EDS micro-area analysis gives Mn 36.2, Al 16.3, Cu 2.6 at.% for the β-Mn in this hardest 17Al sample — i.e. β-Mn is rich in Mn and poor in Al and Cu. HRTEM/FFT confirmed the β-Mn/FCC Cu-rich interface. The overall phase evolution during aging is: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase. This 575 °C/6 h state sits between the incompletely transformed low-temperature states (e.g. 17Al at 525 °C/10 h contains only 20.5 % β-Mn along α grain boundaries) and the fully transformed high-temperature states (≥600 °C, transformed within 1 h).
properties: Vickers microhardness (HVS-1000, 9.8 N for 15 s, average of 5 measurements): 924.9 ± 25.8 HV for this 575 °C/6 h condition — the peak hardness of the 17Al alloy — versus 259.8 ± 1.5 HV for the solution-treated baseline. Along the 575 °C isotherm the hardness climbs from 438.1 ± 39.3 HV (1 h) through 811.7 ± 39.3 HV (3 h) to the 6 h peak, then falls to 831.3 ± 27.4 HV (10 h). Nanoindentation (Agilent G200, 200 nm depth, spacing ≥5 µm) of the hardest 17Al sample gives an average hardness of 11.1 ± 0.6 GPa, and the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn (indents avoiding the softer FCC Cu-rich and BCC particles) is 12.2 ± 0.1 GPa. Elastic modulus (from compressive stress–strain curves) is 175 GPa, and the indentation-derived fracture toughness (Eq. 1, indentation load 9.8 N, average crack length 22 µm) is 6.6 MPa·m¹ᐟ². Density 6.76 g·cm⁻³. No tensile, fatigue or creep data are reported for this sample. Characterization techniques applied: Vickers microhardness testing, nanoindentation, EBSD (IPF + phase mapping, plus FSD), secondary-electron SEM, TEM (BF/DF, SAED, HRTEM, EDS elemental mapping), and XRD (the XRD pattern of the 17Al alloy was taken on the 575 °C/1 h condition, where both α-Mn and β-Mn peaks were found).
mechanisms: Peak hardening is a phase-transformation effect: aging at 575 °C for 6 h drives near-complete α (BCC) → β-Mn transformation, and because β-Mn has a very high intrinsic hardness (measured 12.2 ± 0.1 GPa, >10 GPa) the extensive β-Mn formation raises the alloy from the ~260 HV solution-treated state to the 924.9 HV peak.

β-Mn is a Mn-rich phase, so its nucleation and growth must expel large amounts of Fe, Al and Cu into the surrounding matrix; the resulting enrichment of these atoms around the growing β-Mn hinders further precipitation and growth, which is why higher Al content notably slows the β-Mn precipitation kinetics.
Because Cu has limited solubility in Fe-based alloys and is expelled from β-Mn during its precipitation and growth, Cu redistributes into fine FCC Cu-rich particles that sit at the β-Mn interfaces.
Al enrichment at the β-Mn interfaces — Al being a BCC-stabilizing element — accounts for the formation of the new fine BCC phase within/at the interfaces of β-Mn.
FCC twins form inside the Cu-rich particles (SAED shows two superimposed twin-related patterns), so the interfaces of β-Mn are decorated not only by Cu-rich particles but by internally twinned ones.

Raising the aging temperature accelerates β-Mn precipitation and growth by increasing both the driving force for β-Mn formation and the atomic diffusion rate, so the α→β-Mn transformation shifts to shorter times at higher temperatures (full transformation within 1 h at ≥600 °C versus 6 h at 550 °C and 10 h at 525 °C for 17Al).

The overall hardness depends on both the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn and the absolute volume fraction of β-Mn; as Al increases, the fraction of lower-hardness FCC Cu-rich and BCC precipitates at the β-Mn interfaces grows (3.9 % at 650 °C/3 h for 15Al, 4.7 % at 650 °C/10 h for 17Al, 6.5 % at 650 °C/6 h for 19Al), reducing the β-Mn fraction and thus lowering the attainable hardness.

Fracture toughness falls as Al rises (8.6, 6.6 and 3.5 MPa·m¹ᐟ² for the hardest 15Al, 17Al and 19Al samples) because the slightly harder β-Mn of higher-Al alloys embrittles more readily, while the more ductile FCC Cu-rich phase — which decreases with increasing Al — is progressively replaced by the harder BCC phase.
conclusions: Within the study of Al effects on the aging-hardening behaviour of Fe-35Mn-xAl-5Cu (x = 15, 17, 19 at.%) low-density steels, this 17Al/575 °C/6 h condition is the peak-hardness state of the 17Al alloy (924.9 ± 25.8 HV) and lies in that alloy's optimal ultra-high-hardness window (550–600 °C). Compared with its siblings, the peak hardness decreases with Al content (15Al: 965.6 HV at 600 °C/6 h; 17Al: 924.9 HV at 575 °C/6 h; 19Al: 917.8 HV at 600 °C/10 h), both because β-Mn precipitation kinetics slow with increasing Al and because the fraction of softer FCC Cu-rich and BCC interfacial precipitates grows while fracture toughness falls. The broader significance of the alloy family is that simple short-time aging of low-density Fe-Mn-Al-Cu steels yields an ultra-wide, flexible hardness window (253.4–965.6 HV) via continuous β-Mn precipitation, enabling soft-state forming and subsequent hardening to a target hardness; combined with low density, the Fe-35.2Mn-15.0Al-5.2Cu alloy reaches an ultra-high specific hardness of 141 HV·cm³/g, above existing steels and medium/high-entropy alloys. The remaining limitation is that toughness is still not good enough, and balancing hardness against toughness requires further study.
unmapped: At 575 °C the 17Al alloy hardens rapidly from the start (1 h already gives 438.1 ± 39.3 HV, and the SE-SEM at 575 °C/1 h shows elongated/needle-like contrast within an untransformed α matrix), unlike 15Al/19Al where low-temperature hardening is slower — i.e. the onset of the 17Al response is intermediate between the two sibling alloys.

The XRD pattern used to identify phases in the 17Al alloy corresponds to the 575 °C/1 h condition (not the 6 h peak condition) and showed coincident α-Mn and β-Mn peaks, indicating the two Mn-rich phases co-precipitate before the α matrix fully transforms to β-Mn; the same XRD trace also contains α/D0₃-type reflections.

The 17Al alloy's gating role in the study is that it defines the shift of the optimal ultra-high-hardness aging window: 525–600 °C for 15Al, 550–600 °C for 17Al and 575–625 °C for 19Al, showing the window moves to higher temperature as Al increases.
